text: Two friends come home from Vietnam and one of them no longer believes he is a man. He is in a psychiatric hospital; the other is brought in to talk him back into human company. Alan Parker puts the weight on the visitor rather than the patient, so the two hours run less as a case study than as a negotiation between people who knew each other before the war made either of them unrecognizable. The obsession with birds came first, long before the draft, which blocks the tidy reading that combat alone did this. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix; the National Board of Review counted it among the year's ten best. What stays is smaller than either honor: one man's steady willingness to keep talking to someone who has left the conversation.

The rumor costs nothing to repeat: that a poor family shares a line with the local gentry. A father repeats it, and sends his daughter to the estate to find out what the connection is worth. Roman Polanski takes 172 minutes over what follows and hurries none of it, keeping the errand, the arrival and the slow reckoning of who owes what to whom at the pace of agricultural labor. The film was made in English with French production behind it, and its argument is carried by light and cloth rather than by speech; the Academy Awards it took for cinematography and for costume design are recording structure, not decoration. Class here is a matter of what a body is asked to do outdoors, in weather, for wages. The César for best film followed. The errand is small. Nothing it sets moving is.

The flower is a product, developed to specification, and the specification is happiness. Its chemistry is meant to make the owner content, and the geneticist who bred it gives it more of her attention than she gives her teenage son. Jessica Hausner keeps both facts on the table and lets neither excuse the other. Made in Austria, in English, at 106 minutes, the film treats genetic engineering as work rather than wonder: a variety to be developed, tested, and sold. What stands to be lost is not a life but the reliability of feeling. If contentment can be induced by a scent, nobody in the building can verify that their own is theirs, least of all a woman already unsure whether she loves her child enough. The lead performance took a Best Actress prize; what it plays is nearer to suspicion than to fear.

The orders allow more days than the journey needs, and the surplus is the whole film. Two Navy men are to deliver a young offender to prison, and they decide to give him a good time on the way. Hal Ashby keeps it to 104 minutes and never lets the good time cancel the arithmetic, since every hour of kindness spends what is left. The comedy is genuine. So is the uniform, which is the joke and the trap at once: the men extending the mercy are the men enforcing the sentence, and nothing on the trip alters their assignment. It sits on TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films, earned less by warmth than by structure, a road picture whose destination was fixed by paperwork before anyone got into the car, played by escorts free to be kind and not free to be anything else.

One hundred and sixty-one minutes, most of them inside a single county courtroom. Otto Preminger takes a semi-retired Michigan lawyer's case, a client who disputes not the killing but its meaning, and lets the argument run at the length arguments really run. What is on trial is a word: whether an act can be given a name the law forgives. Nobody is granted the comfort of being obviously right, and Preminger refuses to supply it from outside the frame; the camera watches attorneys work, including the parts of the work that are tactics rather than truth. The wife's account is the case. Both sides know it. The National Film Registry keeps the film and TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films ranks it, and a Volpi Cup went to its lead, a strange and correct honor for a performance assembled almost entirely out of cross-examination.

A writer steps out of a smoke shop, nearly walks into a bus, and is pulled back by a stranger. What follows is arrangement rather than plot: Paul takes Rashid in, Rashid is looking for his father, and Auggie at the counter has learned that a woman who may be his daughter is about to give birth. Wayne Wang lets the three run beside one another for 112 minutes without forcing them to meet, which leaves the shop itself holding the film together, a room where men who owe each other nothing talk anyway. Grief sits close to the surface; Paul's wife was killed, and the film declines to spend that on sentiment. A Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize and a National Board of Review ten-best listing sit on its record. The unit of storytelling is one cigarette long, told across a counter, then repaid with another.

The town is poor, the desert is close, and the woman who left years ago comes back rich. Her offer is exact: her fortune for the town, in exchange for the death of the man who abandoned her and left her with his child. Djibril Diop Mambéty spends the 110 minutes on the deliberation rather than the deed, so the subject becomes what a community will permit itself to want once a price has been said out loud. Wolof, Senegal, 1992. Nothing is concealed from anyone; the sum is public and so is the arithmetic, worked through by people who would have refused it outright on the first morning. Hyènes is ranked on They Shoot Pictures Don't They? 1,000 Greatest Films and holds a Grand Jury Prize. It is also filed as a comedy, and that is not a filing error.

Animation is almost never spent on a grown man's dull week, and here it is spent on nothing else. He talks for a living about how to reach other people, a joke Charlie Kaufman leaves unlabeled, and the event that lifts him is simply that someone he meets is livelier than the rest of his life. Ninety-one minutes. The choice of medium is the argument: a form built for exaggeration handed a story with none, so that every ordinary gesture arrives slightly manufactured, held at the distance of a thing made by hand. A Grand Jury Prize went to it, and the Guardian's 100 Best Films of the 21st Century includes it. It is also funny in the exact way overheard small talk becomes funny when it will not end.

Everything said to the poet reaches him through an interpreter. Andrei Gorchakov is in Italy to research an eighteenth-century Russian composer who once lived abroad, which is a pretext; what he is actually doing is failing to be anywhere. Andrei Tarkovsky shot the film in Italy, in Russian, and the mismatch is the design: an Italian landscape recorded by a man whose measure of a place is elsewhere, with a translator standing between him and every sentence addressed to him. The pace is severe. Shots hold long past the delivery of information, so duration becomes the content, and Domenico, a mystic who believes something can still be redeemed, becomes the one figure willing to act rather than remember. Cannes gave it a directing prize; TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films ranks it. The homesickness is never argued. It is timed.

The inheritance on offer is not money but a job, and the father has one career left in which to arrange it. The mechanism is dull and entirely recognizable, a matter of examinations, favors, a word with the right official, a lifetime of small compliances cashed in at once. Mario Monicelli plays the early stretch for comedy, because a man filling out forms on his child's behalf is funny until the tally of what he will sign comes due. The film took the David di Donatello for best film and belongs to the 100 film italiani da salvare. Italian, 1976, 122 minutes, pitched at office volume throughout. What it finally measures is how short the distance is between a mild man's decency and his complicity: the same habits, the same patience, turned to different use.

Judges are being killed, and the inspector assigned to the case has the least power in it. Francesco Rosi builds the film out of interviews and corridors instead of chases, sending a detective upward through the institutions of the Italian state, where every explanation offered to him is also a maneuver. It is filed as a thriller and paced like a hearing. Because the victims are magistrates, the murders become a question about law rather than about crime, and the investigation's largest obstacle turns out to be that it has been authorized: a man with permission to ask, sent to people with reasons to answer carefully. 121 minutes. It holds the David di Donatello for best film and a place on the 100 film italiani da salvare, and its dread is administrative, accumulated in waiting rooms.

The cameras are small enough to hide in a bag, which is the only reason this footage exists. Anders Østergaard assembled 84 minutes from material shot inside Burma by video journalists for whom filming a street could mean torture or years in prison. The documentary is organized around risk rather than analysis: the question is never what an image means but whether it can be got out of the country, and who stays behind once it has. The reporters are not observers. They are the most exposed people in their own story, and they know that arithmetic before they start recording. A Bodil, a European Film Award for best documentary and a DOX:AWARD are on its record. The honors are Danish and European; the exposure was entirely Burmese.

One night, one strip of road, and a few graduates who are done with school and not yet gone anywhere. George Lucas gives all 112 minutes to that single night, cutting between cars so that no one's evening outranks anyone else's, a structure with no protagonist that was unusual for a 1973 studio comedy and is the reason the film survives its own fondness. Little is at stake except the thing that is wholly at stake: which of them gets into the car that leaves. The talk circles, the driving goes nowhere, and the deadline is never dramatized, because everyone in the frame is already carrying it. AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies includes it and the National Film Registry preserves it. Its comedy is made of people postponing a decision they have in fact already made.

Two thousand dollars is enough to marry on, and enough to be bought with. A young man needs the money for a wedding; the work that pays it turns out to involve killing a woman. Brillante Ma Mendoza gives his 105 minutes to the interval between accepting the job and understanding it, where the pressure sits: a man not yet doing anything, still able to walk away, surrounded by people who know the plan. The subject is consent in installments, not the violence but the chain of small non-refusals that carries an ordinary person from a wedding fund toward a crime, each link defensible by itself. Tagalog dialogue, a French production on paper, 2009. A directing prize went to Mendoza for it. The film is hard by design and the design is not hidden: no relief is offered, and its protagonist's worst quality is that he is agreeable.
